newsitem.title: USA: Miami exiles say they will not enter Cuban airspace.
newsitem.headline: Miami exiles say they will not enter Cuban airspace.

text.p: Cuban exile leaders responded on Friday to U.S. State Department concerns about next week's anniversary of a fatal shootdown by saying they would not fly two military-type aircraft into Cuban air space.
On Monday, anti-Castro exile groups in Miami plan to observe the one-year anniversary of the death of four fliers who were aboard two unarmed Cessna airplanes shot down by Cuban MiG fighter jets.

One of the two military training jets acquired by the exiles will remain parked in Florida and the other will stay well within international airspace off the Florida coast to mark the anniversary, said Ramon Saul Sanchez, head of the exile group known as Democracy Movement.
"We have decided to leave one plane grounded and fly the other just 20 miles (32 km) off the coast in a symbolic gesture," he said.

"There are no remote possibilities that the Cuban government could attempt to justify an attack on the civilian planes conducting the ceremony (by) basing it on the presence of the military aircraft in the general area," he added.
The two Provost military jets still bear the markings of the British Royal Air Force, which used them for training pilots in the 1950s.
On Thursday, the State Department warned exiles and the Cuban government to respect the law during a planned exile demonstration on Monday.
The Cuban-American groups plan to hold a memorial service for the four victims, as well as send private aircraft to drop wreaths over the site of the shootdown.

In addition to the symbolic flight of the fighter jet, the exile groups plan to send an air flotilla of several other single- and twin-engine airplanes into international air space for the anniversary, Sanchez said.

The fatal shooting last year erupted into an international incident when the Cuban government claimed the aircraft were in Cuban airspace but the U.S. government insisted they were over international waters.
A few months later, President Bill Clinton signed into law the Helms-Burton Act that toughened a three-decade-long U.S. economic embargo against Cuba.
